newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: U.S. urges EU not to politicise Boeing deal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges EU not to politicise Boeing deal.

text.p: The United States urged the European Union on Wednesday not to let politics sway its decision on whether aerospace giant Boeing Co.'s planned merger with McDonnell Douglas met its strict antitrust rules.

U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, accompanying President Clinton at the twice yearly U.S.-EU summit, expressed concern that an EU probe into the deal would be dealt with in more than just a commercial manner.
"(We want) assurances that the inquiry must be conducted on competition policy principles and not on extraneous political principles," she told reporters.

U.S. officials said the planned $14 billion merger between the two U.S. airplane manufacturers, one of the most contentious issues in today's trans-Atlantic relations, had not come up directly between Clinton and EU leaders at the summit.
But the officials were clear outside the formal talks that they wanted the European Commission, the EU's antitrust watchdog, to make a straight regulatory decision.
"It is very important that they (the two companies) be judged on purely competition grounds," U.S. Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstadt said.
"It is important to leave the process just as it has traditionally been," he said.
The commission has expressed grave concerns about the effect on competition of Boeing merging with McDonnell Douglas. The deal is also under scrutiny in Washington at the Federal Trade Commission.
Barshefsky underlined, however, that there were differences in the way in which Europe and the United States conduct such antitrust probes.
Washington politicians could not overrule an FTC decision, she said, noting it was a "legal review."
But the 20 European commissioners have the final say over whatever conclusion is reached by their antitrust officials -- hence U.S. fears that Europe could be swayed by political motives.
The commission has expressed concern that the deal would leave the world market with only two major commercial aircraft manufacturers -- Boeing and French-based Airbus Industrie.
Airbus is a consortium of France's Aerospatiale, British Aerospace, Germany's DASA and Spain's Construcciones Aeronautiocas.

The merger would increase Boeing's share of the market for large aircraft -- with a capacity of more than 100 seats -- to 70 percent, given McDonnell's 6 percent share of total aircraft orders at the end of 1996.
The commission, however, is said to be most concerned by Boeing's long-term exclusive supply deals with two U.S. carriers -- AMR Corp.'s American Airlines and Delta Air Lines.
